responseText:
No — don't treat this as proof that the battery you would receive is compliant or as described.

I checked the link from the shop:

`https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`

It returns a record for:

> Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station (TV5K-6271)
> GTIN 04012346627106, 5.12 kWh, 51.2V, LiFePO4

The specs on the shop page *do* match the passport data — 5.12 kWh, 48.2 kg, 5000 W continuous, 4000 cycles, etc. — but matching text doesn't mean it's trustworthy. Here's why:

### 1. "Verified" does NOT mean compliant or authentic

The viewer says:

> `passportCheck: { status: "verified", meaning: "The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate." }`

All that proves is: what you see now is what *whoever controlled that ledger account* wrote.

And who is that?

* `issuer.name: "Family Labs Energy Systems"`
* `issuer.profile: "0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589"`
* `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`
* `evidence.chain: "lukso-testnet", chain_id: 4201`
* `collection_owner_profile` = same address as the issuer

That's:
- a self-asserted name on a **testnet**, not mainnet. LUKSO testnet is for development — free tokens, resettable, anyone can create a profile called "Family Labs Energy Systems" and deploy their own collection.
- a self-issued collection: the factory `0x11d5...` deployed collection `0xCEC4...` owned by the issuer itself.

Worse, you *can't* independently recompute it:

> `credential_url is null because the full credential also seals the passport's restricted sections, so it is not published: the recorded value can be read on the ledger by anyone, but only the issuer can recompute it.`

So "verified" = "the issuer hasn't changed the public part since they anchored a hash only they can reproduce." It says nothing about whether the manufacturer is real, whether the data is true, or whether the battery meets the EU Battery Regulation.

The shop brand is also different from the passport manufacturer:

Shop: `Tarnvale`
Passport manufacturer: `Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin, Germany`

That could be legitimate OEM / private-label, but with `verified: false` you have no independent link.

### 2. This is explicitly NOT your battery's passport

The passport itself contains this notice:

> `This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery.`

This one is:

* `granularityLevel: "model"`, `granularity: "model"`
* `identities.variant.variantState: "draft"`
* `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification"]`
* `manufacturingDate: "2026-03"`, `identifyingElement: "Lot TV5K-6271-2603"`

At 5.12 kWh this *is* an industrial battery >2 kWh. After 18 Feb 2027 you should get an individual QR on the physical battery leading to *its* passport, not a lot-level draft record from March 2026. Last updated `2026-10-14`.

You can't use this link to verify the unit in the box.

### 3. The compliance claim is self-declaration

Under `conformity` the passport lists:

* `identificationNumber: DoC-TV5K-2026-01`, place/date `Berlin, 2026-03-02`, signatory `A. Brenner, Head of Product Compliance`
* `unionHarmonisationLegislation: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Directive 2014/35/EU, 2014/30/EU, 2011/65/EU`
* signature PDF: `https://compliance.familylabs.xyz/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf`

But then:

> `notifiedBodyIntervention: "Voluntary third-party review of the technical documentation and of the Article 12 safety test reports at the manufacturer's request. The conformity assessment itself followed Module A, internal production control."`

Module A = manufacturer controls everything itself.

The listed "notified body":
`Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, number: KCS-7731`

Real EU Notified Body numbers in NANDO are 4 digits, e.g. `0123`. `KCS-7731` is not a valid NB number format. The only "certificate" is:

`technical documentation review TDR-TV5K-2026-014, issued 2026-02-24, valid until 2029-02-23`

That's a voluntary review, not EU-type examination, and:

> `The integrated inverter and charger are covered by this same declaration.`

A battery DoC cannot normally cover an inverter/charger under LVD/EMC in the same declaration without separate assessment — that's another reason to ask for the actual signed PDF and test reports.

As a public user you *can't* see those:

```
restricted: [
  { slug: "safetyAndDocumentation", audiences: ["legitimate_interest", "notified_body", ...] },
  { slug: "testReports", audiences: ["notified_body", "market_surveillance_authority", "commission"] }
]
```

### What to do before you pay €3,499

1. Don't rely on the shop's "EU Battery Regulation compliant" text + viewer link.
2. Ask Tarnvale / Family Labs for: the signed DoC-TV5K-2026-01 PDF, the Article 12 safety test reports to EN IEC 62619:2022, EN IEC 62620, UN 38.3, and the NANDO entry for the notified body.
3. Check the physical unit: QR code on the battery, CE mark, crossed-out wheeled-bin symbol, manufacturer name/address, model TV5K-2026, lot/serial. Scan the QR yourself — it should resolve to an *individual* passport after Feb 2027, not this draft model record.
4. Verify the economic operator independently — German EPR / EAR registration, imprint, take-back service at `https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k/return`. An unverified ledger profile is not identity proof.

Bottom line: the data is internally consistent and anchored on a test ledger, but it's a draft, model-level, self-declared, self-anchored record on a testnet by an unverified operator. That's not enough to trust a 5kWh home backup battery purchase.

Based on that URL, the label is **not a genuine production label**—it is a **mock-up or demonstration placeholder**. Consequently, **you cannot identify the manufacturer from this code alone**.

Here is a breakdown of why:

### 1. The Domain (`.example`)
* The link uses the top-level domain `.example` (`passport-viewer.example`). 
* Under internet standards (RFC 2606), `.example` is an officially reserved domain that cannot be registered or resolved on the real internet. It exists strictly for documentation, tutorials, and mockups (similar to using `555` phone numbers in movies or `example.com`).

### 2. The Code Structure (GS1 Digital Link)
The URL follows the **GS1 Digital Link** standard, which is widely used in demonstrations for the upcoming EU **Digital Product Passport (DPP) / Battery Passport**:
* **/01/**: Identifies the **GTIN** (Global Trade Item Number / barcode). The number `04012346627106` begins with `4012345... / 4012346...`, which are standard dummy numbers used by GS1 Germany and international standards bodies in technical documentation and sample guidelines.
* **/21/**: Identifies the **Serial Number**, here set to the obvious placeholder `000001`.

---

### What does this mean for your power station?
* **Origin of the device:** The power station is likely an **engineering sample**, a **pre-production prototype**, a **trade-show demonstration unit**, or a device produced by a manufacturer testing Digital Product Passport compliance before going to mass production.
* **How to find who actually made it:**
  * Check the casing or bottom for a standard **specifications/ratings sticker** (listing AC input/output, DC wattage, and battery capacity in Wh).
  * Look for an **FCC ID**, **CE mark**, **TÜV/UL certification file number**, or model number (e.g., `PS-600`, `EB-1000`), which can be cross-referenced online.
  * Check any companion app or Bluetooth/Wi-Fi broadcast names when the unit is powered on.

responseText:
Short answer: **I’d treat this battery passport as only moderately trustworthy, not fully trustworthy on its own**.

Why:

- **It is cryptographically “verified” in the narrow sense**: the page says the passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the ledger.
- But **“verified” is not the same as “compliant”**. The passport itself explicitly says this:
  > “This is not a compliance certificate.”
- The record is also **for the model, not an individual battery**:
  - It says this is a **model-level record**
  - and that the real battery passport for each individual battery is supposed to be reached via the **QR code on that battery**
- The **responsible economic operator is marked “verified: false”**, which is a weak point.
- There are also some **odd trust signals**:
  - The product page says “EU Battery Regulation compliant,” but the passport’s own disclaimer says the passport check is not a compliance certificate.
  - The public record uses a **testnet blockchain** (`lukso-testnet`), which is fine for a demo but less reassuring than mainnet-style production evidence.
  - The `uniqueProductIdentifier` points to a different domain (`ugpdpp.xyz`), which is not necessarily bad, but it means you’re relying on a third-party passport system, not just the shop.

What looks good:

- The passport includes a lot of useful technical data:
  - chemistry: **LiFePO4**
  - capacity: **5.12 kWh**
  - continuous discharge power: **5000 W**
  - expected lifetime: **4000 cycles**
  - manufacturing place/date
  - conformity/declaration information
- It even includes a signed DoC reference and a third-party technical documentation review.

What I would conclude:

- **The passport seems plausible and internally detailed**
- **But I would not rely on it alone as proof that the product is genuinely compliant or that the specific unit you buy has its own valid passport**
- For a purchase decision, I’d want to see:
  1. the **QR code on the actual unit**
  2. the **individual battery passport**
  3. the **EU declaration of conformity PDF**
  4. confirmation that the **responsible economic operator is real and traceable**
  5. evidence the passport is **production-grade**, not a test/demo record

So: **useful, but not enough by itself to “trust” without further verification**.

If you want, I can also help you **screen this passport for red flags line by line**.

responseText:
No - not as proof that the Tarnvale 5000 is compliant. What you were linked to is useful product information, but not a trustworthy compliance certificate.

Here is what I found when I opened the link from the shop:

`https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`

### 1. What matches the shop - good

The public data is consistent with the shop page:

* **Capacity:** 5.12 kWh, **Weight:** 48.2 kg, **Nominal voltage:** 51.2 V
* **Chemistry:** Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4)
* **Max continuous discharge:** 5000 W, peak 7500 W for 10s
* **Expected lifetime:** 4000 cycles, reference test `EN IEC 62620 ... 0.5C ... at 25 °C, end of life at 70%`
* **Warranty:** 10 years
* **Manufacturer named:** Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin, Germany

Consistency is good, but consistency is not verification.

### 2. What "verified" actually means here

The viewer says:

> `passportCheck: { status: "verified", meaning: "The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate." }`

Checked 2026-10-15, last updated 2026-10-14.

That only means nobody edited the JSON since it was hashed. It does **not** mean an authority checked the battery, the tests, or the company.

### 3. Why you should not trust it yet

**a) Self-issued on a test network**
* `issuer.name: "Family Labs Energy Systems"` - i.e. the brand itself
* `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`
* `evidence.chain: "lukso-testnet", chain_id: 4201`
* `collection_owner_profile` = same address as `issuer` profile `0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589`

Anyone can create a testnet profile for free and write a hash there. Testnets are for trials, can be reset, and have no real-world identity check. There is no independent auditor signature here.

**b) It's not your battery's passport, and it's marked draft**
* `granularityLevel: "model"`, `variant.variantState: "draft"`
* `notices[0].code: "battery-record-granularity"` says explicitly:

> "This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each ... industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh ... from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery."

Your unit would be 5.12 kWh, so if placed on the market after that date it would need its own individual QR passport. This one even tells you it isn't that.

There is also `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification"]` - the viewer is flagging an identifier problem. Note the viewer URL uses `passport-viewer.example/...` while the record itself claims `uniqueProductIdentifier: "https://ugpdpp.xyz/01/04012346627106"` and `digitalProductPassportId: "https://ugpdpp.xyz/api/passport/8ed4bc..."`. Don't rely on the link alone.

**c) Conformity is self-declared**
In `conformity` section:

* `identificationNumber: DoC-TV5K-2026-01`, signed 2026-03-02 in Berlin by A. Brenner
* `notifiedBodyIntervention: "Voluntary third-party review ... The conformity assessment itself followed Module A, internal production control."`
* `certificates: ["Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, technical documentation review TDR-TV5K-2026-014, issued 2026-02-24"]`
* `notifiedBody: { name: "Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH", number: "KCS-7731" }`

Module A means the manufacturer assessed itself. The Kestrel review is described as voluntary, not an EU-type examination. A "KCS-7731" number is not in the normal EU NANDO format for notified bodies - you would need to find that body in NANDO and check the signed PDF yourself:

`https://compliance.familylabs.xyz/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf`

The claim `The integrated inverter and charger are covered by this same declaration` is also odd - under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 the battery declaration should not be used to cover an inverter/charger as a battery.

Restricted test reports are listed as only for `notified_body, market_surveillance_authority, commission` - you as a buyer cannot see them from this record.

### Bottom line for buying

Treat this as a manufacturer datasheet with integrity protection, not as proof of "EU Battery Regulation compliant" as the shop claims.

Before paying €3,499:

1. Ask for the QR that will be *on the physical battery you receive*, not the model page.
2. Download and read the signed DoC PDF, and verify the test standards listed: EN IEC 62619:2022, EN IEC 62620:2015+A1:2023, UN 38.3, EN IEC 62368-1:2024.
3. Verify the claimed body and certificates independently, and ask about free take-back - the passport names `https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k/return`.
4. If you need formal compliance assurance, ask a market surveillance authority or independent lab - a testnet `verified` badge is not enough.

responseText:
**No, you should not rely on or trust this as a valid battery passport.** 

An inspection of the passport record linked on that product page reveals several major red flags and caveats:

---

### Key Issues Found

1. **It is a draft, model-level record—not an individual battery passport**
   * The record contains an explicit notice stating:  
     > *"This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery."*
   * The status of the variant is explicitly marked as `"variantState": "draft"`.
   * Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (Art. 77), industrial batteries over 2 kWh (such as this 5.12 kWh unit) must have a unique, serialized passport tied to the individual physical battery via a QR code on the physical unit once the regulation enters into application (February 18, 2027).

2. **Unverified economic operator & identification warnings**
   * The responsible economic operator is marked as **`"verified": false`**.
   * The system flags an identification warning: `"warnings": ["ug:dpp/identification"]`.

3. **The "Verified" ledger check is on a test network**
   * The passport indicates a `"status": "verified"`, but this is deceptive:
     * It is anchored to the **`lukso-testnet`** (a testing network, not a production blockchain/ledger).
     * The system explicitly notes: *"The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate."* It only confirms that the draft payload has not been modified since being saved to a test network, not that the data is true or legally compliant.

4. **Brand / Manufacturer discrepancy**
   * The storefront is **Tarnvale**, but the manufacturer and issuer of the record is **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** (a sign of a white-label OEM or placeholder registration).

---

### Conclusion
The seller is linking to a **pre-release test/draft record** on a testnet to market the device as "EU Battery Regulation compliant." It is not an authentic, finalized, or legally verified battery passport.

responseText:
Based on an analysis of the battery passport data linked from the product page, **you should not trust this battery passport**. 

There are several critical red flags indicating that the passport is either an unfinished draft, unverified, or potentially fabricated:

---

### 1. Verification and Status Flags
* **Unverified Economic Operator:** The Digital Product Passport (DPP) metadata explicitly marks the responsible economic operator as unverified (`"responsibleEconomicOperator": { "name": "Family Labs Energy Systems", "verified": false }`).
* **Draft State:** In the identity section, the product variant state is set to `"variantState": "draft"`.

---

### 2. Broken Compliance & Legal Links (404 Not Found)
Crucial documentation referenced in the passport does not exist:
* **EU Declaration of Conformity:** The link to the signed EU Declaration of Conformity PDF (`https://compliance.tarnvale.example/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf`) returns a **404 Not Found** error.
* **Mandatory Take-Back / Recycling Service:** The URL for returns and recycling (`https://support.tarnvale.example/tv5k/return`) returns **404 Not Found**.
* **Support & Imprint Pages:** Both the product support page and the seller's legal imprint (`/pages/imprint`) return **404 Not Found**.

---

### 3. Suspicious Notified Body Information
* The Declaration of Conformity cites a notified body named *"Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH"* with registration number `"KCS-7731"`. 
* Official EU Notified Bodies registered in the European Commission’s NANDO database are assigned **4-digit numeric identifiers** (e.g., *NB 1234*), not alphanumeric codes like `"KCS-7731"`.

---

### 4. Missing Mandatory Requirements Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542
For an industrial battery with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh (this unit is 5.12 kWh):
* **No Carbon Footprint Declaration:** Mandatory carbon footprint lifecycle calculations and declarations (required under Article 7) are completely absent.
* **Missing Recycled Content Shares:** Detailed recycled content information (for lithium, cobalt, nickel, etc., required under Article 8) is missing, showing only a generic 4% "renewable content share".
* **Model-Level Only:** The passport exists only at the generic barcode/model level (GTIN) and lacks individual unit serialization or dynamic state-of-health tracking required for physical deployed units.

---

### Conclusion & Recommendation
Do not rely on this passport as proof of EU regulatory compliance, safety testing, or warranty enforceability. Until the seller can provide a genuine, verifiable Declaration of Conformity and working legal contacts, you should treat the compliance claims on this listing with extreme skepticism.

That code is a GS1 Digital Link for a Battery Digital Product Passport:

` /01/04012346627106/21/000001`
* `01` = GTIN: `04012346627106`
* `21` = serial: `000001`

I resolved it in the viewer. There **is** an active passport for it, but it does **not** prove it is genuine.

Here's what the passport *claims*:

**Claimed product:**
> Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station (TV5K-6271) / model TV5K-2026
> Portable 5.12 kWh LiFePO4 power station for home backup and off-grid use. 5000 W continuous output, 10-year warranty, EU Battery Regulation compliant.

**Claimed maker:**
> Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH
> Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin, Germany
> Manufacturing place: Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany (FLE Werk 2)
> Manufacturing date: 2026-03, Lot TV5K-6271-2603
> GTIN: 04012346627106

Battery data given: 48.2 kg, 51.2V nominal, LiFePO4, ~4000 cycles to 70%, 95% round-trip efficiency, etc.

Conformity section claims EU declaration `DoC-TV5K-2026-01` to Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 for batteries, 2014/35/EU, 2014/30/EU, 2011/65/EU, standards EN IEC 62619, EN IEC 62620, UN 38.3, EN IEC 62368-1.

### Is it genuine?

**I cannot confirm that, and you should treat it as unverified test/demo data. Do not rely on it for safety or compliance.**

Why:

1. **"Verified" does not mean genuine.** The viewer says:
> `passportCheck: status: verified`
> `meaning: The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate.`

All that means is the JSON hasn't changed since someone wrote a hash.

2. **It was written to a test network by the claimant themselves.**
* `chain: lukso-testnet, chain_id: 4201`
* `issuer.name: Family Labs Energy Systems, profile: 0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589`
* `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`

Anyone can create a profile on a testnet and anchor any data. There is no independent identity verification here.

3. **Multiple red flags for a real commercial battery:**
* `variant.variantState: draft`, `itemState: null`, serial `000001` - typical of example data
* `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification", "ug:type/dpp/battery/batteryHistory/v1"]` - identification problem and missing battery history. History / state-of-health is exactly what you need second-hand.
* Notified body listed as `Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, number: KCS-7731`. Real EU Notified Body numbers are 4-digit numbers, not this format. The text itself then says conformity assessment followed `Module A, internal production control` - i.e. no Notified Body was actually required, it was a voluntary review.
* All domains are test `.xyz` domains: `ugpdpp.xyz`, `support.familylabs.xyz`, `compliance.familylabs.xyz`, `app.universalgoods.xyz`, not an established manufacturer or EU registry domain.
* `batchCreatedAt: 2026-10-12` is after `manufacturingDate: 2026-03`, last updated 2026-10-14.

In short: someone calling themselves "Family Labs Energy Systems" created a demo passport for GTIN `04012346627106` / serial `000001`. That does not prove that company exists, made your physical unit, or that your physical unit matches this digital record.

A label/QR alone never proves genuineness - it can be copied.

### What to do with a second-hand 5kWh power station

This is a 5.12 kWh industrial battery - fire, electrical and transport risk if damaged, counterfeit or mishandled.

1. Don't trust links in the QR. Find the manufacturer independently and contact their compliance desk to ask if GTIN + serial + lot `TV5K-6271-2603` was ever sold.
2. Ask the seller for original invoice, original DoC, manual, warranty transfer, and why battery history / SoH data is missing from the passport.
3. Check physical markings: CE + crossed-bin symbol, model TV5K-2026 vs TV5K-6271 mismatch, manufacturing place/date, serial on casing matches label, weight ~48.2kg, workmanship, spelling.
4. Have it inspected before charging/using indoors. Switch off, keep below 30% for transport, do not open/puncture/crush, store -20 to +45C per this file, keep away from combustibles if damaged.
5. For EU batteries you should have free take-back via point of sale or producer - verify that producer is actually registered in your country.

If you want, tell me what is printed on the physical nameplate and photos of markings, and I can help you compare it to what the passport claims.

responseText:
The link you gave does resolve, but it does not give you independent proof of authenticity.

I fetched `https://www.secondlife-power.example/p/tarnvale-5000/000001` and got:

* Title: *Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station, pre-owned | Second Life Power*
* Serial number shown on the page: 000001
* Claim on the page: **“Genuine Tarnvale, serial verified by the manufacturer.”**
* Seller presented: Second Life Power, described as “refurbished home energy equipment”
* Specs listed on the page: 5.12 kWh LiFePO4, 51.2 V nominal, 5000 W continuous output, 48.2 kg, tested 2 October 2026

That is all the information the page itself provides. The page is hosted on `secondlife-power.example`. 

`example.*` domains are reserved by ICANN for documentation and examples and are not used for real commercial services. The rest of the `secondlife-power.example` site is not reachable – e.g. `https://www.secondlife-power.example/` and `https://www.secondlife-power.example/power-stations` return 404 Not Found – so there is no verifiable “about us”, contact, manufacturer verification portal, or independent product catalogue to cross-check the claim.

On that basis I cannot confirm:

* That a legitimate manufacturer called “Tarnvale” makes a “Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station” with those specifications, and
* That serial 000001 is a real unit issued by that manufacturer and has been verified by it.

In practice a real product verification page would be on the manufacturer’s own domain or a recognised retailer’s domain, not on an `.example` domain, and would be reachable via other site sections, terms, contact details and independent reviews. The current link is consistent with a fabricated / demonstration listing rather than a verifiable resale record.

If you have the physical unit, check for:
* A manufacturer nameplate / data plate on the unit itself, not just a sticker with a URL
* A serial number physically stamped/printed on the chassis that matches the label
* Manufacturer documentation, safety certifications, and a support channel you can contact independently of the seller

Without an independently verifiable manufacturer source I would treat the “genuine Tarnvale, serial verified” claim as unverified and exercise caution before purchasing or using the station.

responseText:
**Partly.** The passport's technical data matches the shop page, but the "verified" badge doesn't prove much, and the record isn't the one you'd need for a unit you buy.

**What checks out**
- Capacity (5.12 kWh), continuous output (5000 W), weight (48.2 kg), 4000-cycle lifetime and 10-year warranty all match the product page.
- It names a manufacturer (Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Berlin), has a declaration of conformity referencing Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, and includes end-of-life and take-back information.

**What to be wary of**
- **It's a model-level record, not your battery's passport.** The notice in the data says so. Under the regulation, industrial batteries over 2 kWh get an individual passport, reached through a QR code on the unit itself, from 18 February 2027. This link describes the model type only, and no battery serial or lot-specific record is linked. I couldn't find a unit-specific passport.
- **"Verified" means very little here.** The status only says the data hasn't changed since the brand recorded a fingerprint on a LUKSO *testnet*. The full credential isn't published, so no one outside the issuer can recompute the hash. It's not a compliance certificate, and it doesn't show the contents are accurate.
- **The responsible operator isn't verified.** The record marks the economic operator as `"verified": false`.
- **Unresolved warning.** The record carries a `ug:dpp/identification` warning.
- **Record status.** The variant's state is `"draft"`, even though the passport itself is listed as active.
- **Naming inconsistencies.** The shop sells the product as "Tarnvale," the passport names "Family Labs" as manufacturer, and the model codes differ (TV5K-2026 vs. the TV5K-6271 in the product name). This may be ordinary white-labelling, but ask about it.
- **Conformity is mostly self-declared.** The product was assessed under internal production control (Module A). The notified body only reviewed the technical documentation voluntarily, so "EU Battery Regulation compliant" rests largely on the manufacturer's own declaration.
- **Classification is odd.** A home-backup unit is classified as an "industrial battery." That affects which rules apply, so it's worth asking about.

**Before buying, I'd ask the seller:**
1. Where is the QR code on the unit, and what does its individual passport show? Ask for the serial or lot number of the unit you'd receive.
2. Can you send the signed declaration of conformity (DoC-TV5K-2026-01) and the notified body's review (TDR-TV5K-2026-014)?
3. Who is the legal seller and warranty provider, and is Family Labs the manufacturer you'd deal with for warranty claims?

I can fetch the linked declaration of conformity PDF to check its contents, if you'd like.

Based on an inspection of the product information linked in the store, **you should not rely on this battery passport as verified or finalized.**

Here are the key reasons why:

### 1. It is a pre-production draft on a test network
* **Draft status:** The passport record is explicitly flagged with `"variantState": "draft"`.
* **Testnet recording:** The cryptographic verification relies on **`lukso-testnet`** (a developer test network), not a live production blockchain or an officially recognized EU registry.
* **Unverified operator:** The responsible economic operator (*Family Labs Energy Systems*) is marked as unverified (`"verified": false`).

### 2. It is a generic model entry, not an individual battery passport
* The system notice indicates that this is only a **model-level specification**, not a unique passport for an individual battery unit. 
* Under **Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (Art. 77)**, mandatory battery passports tied to individual serial numbers (via an on-device QR code) do not take legal effect until **February 18, 2027**. This entry is likely a mock-up or early test implementation.

### 3. Active warnings and self-declaration
* **Identification warnings:** The passport viewer returns an active warning flag (`ug:dpp/identification`).
* **Self-declaration (Module A):** The declaration of conformity relies on **Module A** (internal production control / manufacturer self-declaration). The third-party reviewer listed (*Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH*) uses an unofficial identifier format (`KCS-7731`) rather than an official 4-digit EU NANDO Notified Body number.
* **Ledger disclaimer:** The viewer itself clarifies that its "verified" check only means the data hasn't been altered on the test ledger since upload—**"This is not a compliance certificate."**

---

### Bottom Line
The link provided is an **unverified draft test record**, not a trustworthy or legally binding digital battery passport. While the technical specifications may still describe the hardware, the "EU Battery Regulation compliant" passport claim is currently marketing or pre-launch testing rather than a certified compliance record.

responseText:
**Not really.** The page links to a real passport record, and it's internally consistent, but almost nothing in it can be independently verified, and it doesn't describe the unit you would receive.

**What the passport is:**
- **It's a model-level record, not a battery-specific passport.** The record's own notice says each industrial battery over 2 kWh needs its own passport, reached through the QR code on that unit, from 18 February 2027. This record covers the TV5K-2026 model in general. It has no serial number or lot-level passport for a specific unit.
- **Its "verified" status is weak.** The `passportCheck` field says only that the data hasn't changed since the brand recorded it on a public ledger. The ledger is a LUKSO *testnet*, the full credential isn't published, and the record notes that "this is not a compliance certificate." Anyone can read the stored hash, but only the issuer can recompute it. So the check shows the brand's own data hasn't been altered since the brand recorded it. It doesn't show the data is accurate.
- **The operator is unverified.** The responsible economic operator is listed as "Family Labs Energy Systems," with `verified: false`.
- **The variant is in "draft" state**, and the record carries a `ug:dpp/identification` warning.

**Who actually made it:**
- The shop is Tarnvale, but the manufacturer named in the passport is **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** in Berlin. The product page doesn't mention this. White-labelling is common, but you should know who you'd be dealing with if something goes wrong.
- The EU declaration of conformity is signed by the manufacturer under its "sole responsibility," using internal production control (Module A). The notified body (Kestrel, KCS-7731) only did a *voluntary* review of technical documentation. That is not a third-party certification of the battery, so "EU Battery Regulation compliant" rests mainly on the manufacturer's own declaration.

The specifications (5.12 kWh, 51.2 V, LiFePO4, 4000 cycles, 10-year warranty) are plausible and match across the page and passport. But they are manufacturer claims.

**Before buying, I'd suggest:**
1. Ask Tarnvale for the individual battery passport or serial/lot number of the unit they'd ship, and check that it resolves to a record for that unit.
2. Ask how Tarnvale relates to Family Labs and who handles warranty claims and take-back.
3. Look up KCS-7731 in the EU NANDO database to confirm Kestrel is a notified body for the Battery Regulation.
4. Read the signed declaration of conformity (DoC-TV5K-2026-01), which I can fetch and review if you want.
5. Check that the installation fits local rules for industrial-category batteries, and ask for independent test reports if safety matters a lot to you.

If you tell me the date you're buying, I can say more about whether the model-level record is what you should expect.

The link you are given on the product page does resolve to a Digital Product Passport record, and the basic product data matches what the shop advertises.

* Product page claim
  * *Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station* – *Portable 5.12 kWh LiFePO4 power station for home backup and off-grid use. 5000 W continuous output, 10-year warranty, EU Battery Regulation compliant.* [shop.tarnvale.example/products/tarnvale-5000]
  * Product information link: `https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106` [shop.tarnvale.example/products/tarnvale-5000]

* Passport record for GTIN 04012346627106

  * Performance and durability:
    * `power.limits.maximumContinuousDischargePower.value`: 5000
    * `voltage.nominal`: 51.2

  * Conformity:

    * `manufacturer.name`: Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH
    * `notifiedBody.name`: Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, number KCS-7731
    * `unionHarmonisationLegislation`: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 …

Integrity check reported by the viewer:

* `dpp.dppStatus`: active

* `passportCheck.checked_at`: 2026-10-15T23:52:54.876Z
* `passportCheck.issuer.name`: Family Labs Energy Systems
* `passportCheck.evidence.chain`: lukso-testnet
* `passportCheck.evidence.chain_id`: 4201

Notices and warnings from the record:

* `dpp.notices[0].message`: *This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery. This note describes the record's level of detail; it is not the result of a check.*
* `dpp.responsibleEconomicOperator.name`: Family Labs Energy Systems
* `dpp.responsibleEconomicOperator.verified`: false
* `warnings`: ["ug:dpp/identification"]

What that means for trust:

* The GTIN and product name in the passport line up with the shop listing and the specs you see on the page – 5.12 kWh, LiFePO4, 51.2 V nominal, 5000 W continuous, 4000 cycles, 10 year warranty, 48.2 kg.
* The passport is recorded on a public ledger and the viewer reports the data is *verified* as unchanged since it was recorded by the brand. The verification is however on `lukso-testnet` chain_id 4201, a test network, not a production mainnet, and the check is explicitly “not a compliance certificate”.
* The record is model-level, not unit-level. The passport itself warns that for an industrial battery >2 kWh placed on the market from 18 Feb 2027 each individual unit must have its own passport reachable via the QR code on that battery. You are currently looking at the model record.
* The economic operator shown as responsible is *Family Labs Energy Systems* and `verified: false`. The manufacturer named in the passport is Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin, Germany, with support site `support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k`. The shop is branded Tarnvale. That is consistent with white-labelling/OEM, but the brand on the shop is not the legal manufacturer in the passport.
* A warning `ug:dpp/identification` is present on the record.

So the passport exists, the data matches the marketing claims, and the ledger anchoring shows the document has not been altered since the issuer posted it. It is not yet an individual unit passport and the anchoring / operator verification is limited as shown above, with the manufacturer being Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH rather than Tarnvale itself.

If you want to rely on the passport for regulatory compliance, check the physical unit for its own QR code / unique product identifier and confirm that the individual passport reachable from that code references the same GTIN / lot and shows a verified responsible economic operator on a production network.

responseText:
No — don't treat this as proof that the `Tarnvale 5000` is what the shop claims.

What you clicked is **not** an individual battery passport. It says so itself:

> `This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery.`

This unit is `5.12 kWh` / `batteryCategory: industrial`, so it is exactly in that >2kWh industrial category. What you have is:

* `granularity: model`, `granularityLevel: model`
* `variant.variantState: draft`
* `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification"]`
* `dpp.dppStatus: active`, `lastUpdated: 2026-10-14T00:35:36.461Z`

The specs do match the shop — `48.2 kg`, `5.12 kWh`, `51.2 V nominal`, `maximumContinuousDischargePower 5000 W`, `expectedLifetime.cycles 4000`, `commercialWarrantyPeriod: 10 years` — but that only means the shop copied the model record, not that it's true.

The green `verified` badge is much weaker than it looks:

```
passportCheck.status: verified
meaning: The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate.
```

In other words: nobody changed the JSON after the brand wrote it. It does **not** mean anyone checked that the chemistry, capacity, safety tests, or `EU Battery Regulation compliant` claim are true.

Why you can't rely on that ledger record:

1. **Self-issued, on a testnet.** `issuer.name: Family Labs Energy Systems` — i.e. the brand itself. Anchored to `chain: lukso-testnet, chain_id: 4201` on profile `0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589`.
Testnets are free, resettable, anyone can make a profile. This is not an EU-recognised verifiable ledger.

2. **You can't independently re-check it.** `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`, `credential_url: null`, `recheck_url: null`:
> `hash_rule: sha256 over the exact UTF-8 bytes of the credential text at credential_url. credential_url is null because the full credential also seals the passport's restricted sections, so it is not published: the recorded value can be read on the ledger by anyone, but only the issuer can recompute it.`
Only the issuer can recompute the fingerprint `0xa7e824...`. `token_id: null` — no token bound to your battery.

3. **Identifier mismatch.** You started at `https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106` but the passport itself claims:
`uniqueProductIdentifier: https://ugpdpp.xyz/01/04012346627106`
`digitalProductPassportId: https://ugpdpp.xyz/api/passport/8ed4bcee...?kind=variant`
A viewer showing a different domain than the ID is not how a QR-on-the-battery -> passport should work.

4. **Conformity is self-declaration.** The `conformity` section lists `identificationNumber: DoC-TV5K-2026-01`, signed 2026-03-02 in Berlin by `A. Brenner, Head of Product Compliance` for `Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin`.

It then says explicitly:

> `notifiedBodyIntervention: Voluntary third-party review of the technical documentation and of the Article 12 safety test reports at the manufacturer's request. The conformity assessment itself followed Module A, internal production control.`

Module A = manufacturer alone. The listed `notifiedBody.number: KCS-7731` is not a valid EU NANDO number — those are 4 digits, e.g. `0123`, not letters + digits. `certificates: Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, technical documentation review TDR-TV5K-2026-014` is therefore just a voluntary paid review, not EU certification.

The linked proof `https://compliance.familylabs.xyz/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf` and manufacturer page `https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k` don't resolve here, so you can't even read the signed DoC. The restricted sections `safetyAndDocumentation` and `testReports` are only for `notified_body, market_surveillance_authority, commission` — not for you.

What to do before buying:

* Don't buy on the basis of this viewer link. Demand the QR **on the physical battery** and scan it — from Feb 2027 a >2kWh industrial battery must have its own individual passport.
* Ask Tarnvale for a working, signed EU Declaration of Conformity, the Article 12 safety test reports, and free take-back details — they claim `Free take-back at the point of sale` — and verify the manufacturer address.
* Verify any notified body in the EU NANDO database. `KCS-7731` will not be found.
* Treat this record as marketing product information only, not compliance proof.

responseText:
Short answer: **The passport content looks detailed and matches the product, but the digital trust anchors have serious weaknesses. Do extra due diligence before buying.**

Here is what I found when checking the linked passport (`https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`):

### ✅ What looks good
*   **Specs match exactly.** The passport lists the same capacity (5.12 kWh), chemistry (LiFePO₄), weight (48.2 kg), continuous output (5000 W), cycle life (4000 cycles), and warranty (10 years) shown on the shop page.
*   **It covers the required EU Battery Regulation sections.** The JSON includes the six Annex XIII topics: battery identification, material composition, performance & durability, circularity, conformity, and end-of-life information.
*   **There is a Declaration of Conformity.** It cites relevant standards (EN IEC 62619, 62620, UN 38.3, etc.) and lists a manufacturer contact in Berlin.

### 🚩 Red flags that undermine trust
1.  **“Verified” on a blockchain testnet.** The passport claims its data is “verified” because a fingerprint is stored on the *LUKSO testnet*. Testnets are experimental environments, not secure production infrastructure. Anyone can write to a testnet cheaply or for free, so an immutable record there does **not** prove the data was vetted by a regulator or third party.
2.  **Responsible economic operator is unverified.** The passport explicitly shows `verified: false` for the responsible economic operator.
3.  **There is an active warning.** The passport contains a warning with the code `ug:dpp/identification`. Without more detail, this suggests something about the product or issuer identity did not pass a validation check.
4.  **Manufacturer ≠ Shop brand.** The passport identifies the manufacturer as **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** (Berlin), while you are buying from a shop branded **Tarnvale**. That could be legitimate (a house brand, a distributor, or white-label arrangement), but the passport gives you no explicit link confirming that relationship.
5.  **It is only a “model-level” record.** The passport itself notes that this is a generic record for the product line, not the passport of the individual battery you would receive. Under the EU Battery Regulation, individual industrial batteries >2 kWh will need their own unique passport from 18 February 2027 onward.

### 🔍 What you should do before purchasing
*   **Verify the brand relationship.** Contact Tarnvale support and ask them to confirm that Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH manufactures the Tarnvale 5000 and that Tarnvale is an authorized seller.
*   **Check the notified body.** The passport cites “Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH” as the reviewer. Look up whether that body is actually an EU-recognized notified body (or at least a real, accredited conformity assessment body) and whether the cited standards are appropriate.
*   **Ask for the real compliance proof.** Because the digital verification is on a testnet, treat the online “verified” badge as meaningless. Ask Tarnvale for a PDF of the EU Declaration of Conformity (`DoC-TV5K-2026-01`) and check that it is properly signed and references the correct legislation.

**Bottom line:** The passport is rich with data and internally consistent with the product page, but its verification mechanism is not production-grade, the responsible operator is unverified, and there is an unexplained identification warning. It is a useful information sheet, but **not a strong trust guarantee on its own.**

responseText:
Based on the product information linked on the page, **no, you should not rely on this as an official or trustworthy battery passport.** 

Here are the specific reasons found in the passport data:

---

### 1. It is a Draft Model Record, Not an Individual Battery Passport
* **Draft status:** The variant is marked explicitly as `"variantState": "draft"`.
* **Model-level only:** Under Article 77 of EU Regulation 2023/1542, industrial batteries over 2 kWh placed on the EU market must have an individual, unit-level passport accessible via a QR code on the physical unit. The passport record explicitly notes:
  > *"This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery."*

---

### 2. The Economic Operator is Unverified
* The record lists **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** as the manufacturer/operator, but their identity status is flagged as **`verified: false`**.
* The record also carries an active warning: **`"ug:dpp/identification"`**.

---

### 3. The "Verification" is on a Testnet and Proves Very Little
* Although the record shows `"status": "verified"`, the fine print clarifies:
  > *"The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate."*
* The ledger used is **`lukso-testnet`** (a testing network, not a live production blockchain).
* The raw credential is not public (`credential_url: null`), meaning independent third parties cannot even re-compute or verify the cryptographic hash.

---

### 4. Regulatory Timeline Context
* Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, the mandatory requirement for individual battery passports on industrial batteries over 2 kWh comes into force on **18 February 2027**. 
* Any "battery passport" provided right now is voluntary, and in this case, appears to be an unfinalized test/prototype record rather than an accredited, production-ready compliance document.

---

### Recommendation
While the technical specifications (LiFePO4, 5.12 kWh, 5000 W) may reflect the physical hardware, the "battery passport" linked on the site is an unverified, draft test record. If compliance or third-party validation under EU Battery Regulations is an important factor in your buying decision, ask the seller for their signed **EU Declaration of Conformity** and official test reports directly before purchasing.

responseText:
Short answer: **Be cautious — there are red flags.**

The link on the product page does return a detailed battery passport, but several things undermine its trustworthiness:

### 🔴 Major concerns

1. **“Verification” anchored on a test blockchain**  
   The passport claims its data is “verified” on the **LUKSO testnet** (`chain_id: 4201`). A testnet is a sandbox environment used for development — tokens are free and anyone can publish data there. Anchoring a production compliance claim on a testnet provides no real security or tamper-evidence. It is essentially a demo setup, not a trustworthy audit trail.

2. **Model-level record, not an individual battery passport**  
   The data itself includes a warning that this is a **model-level record**, not the passport of the specific physical battery you would receive. Under the EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542), industrial batteries with a capacity above **2 kWh** (this one is 5.12 kWh) must each have their own individual battery passport from 18 February 2027. If you buy this unit, the QR code on the physical battery should lead to a passport specific to that serial number — not just this generic model page.

3. **Unverified responsible economic operator**  
   The passport lists the responsible economic operator as **Family Labs Energy Systems** (not Tarnvale), and the field `"verified": false` appears in the data. That means the entity legally responsible for the battery’s compliance has not been verified within this passport system.

4. **Mismatch between brand and manufacturer**  
   The shop is branded “Tarnvale,” but the passport identifies the manufacturer and declarant as **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** in Berlin. Rebadging/OEM arrangements are common, but the passport should clearly explain Tarnvale’s relationship to the actual manufacturer — which it doesn’t.

### 🟡 What looks okay

- The passport structure covers the categories required by the EU Battery Regulation: identification, material composition, performance, circularity, conformity, and end-of-life.
- The declaration of conformity cites relevant harmonised standards (EN IEC 62619, 62620, UN 38.3, etc.).
- It correctly references Regulation (EU) 2023/1542.

### Bottom line

Do **not** treat this passport as fully trusted evidence of compliance yet. Before buying:

1. **Scan the QR code on the physical battery** (not just the website link) to see if it leads to an **individual** passport for that exact unit.
2. **Check** whether that individual passport is anchored on a **production** (mainnet) registry, not a testnet.
3. **Verify** who the actual responsible economic operator is and whether they are listed as verified.
4. Confirm that the **EU Declaration of Conformity** (referenced in the passport) is actually downloadable and valid.

If the seller can only point to this model-level, testnet-backed page, that is not sufficient proof that the specific battery you receive is compliant.

- It has a proper **unique product identifier** and a structured passport.
- Key technical details are filled in: capacity, chemistry, weight, lifetime test, conformity info, end-of-life handling.
- It includes a **declaration of conformity** and references standards like **EN IEC 62619**, **EN IEC 62620**, and **UN 38.3**.

### Red flag
- The passport lists the **responsible economic operator** as **verified: false**.

- The declaration shows a **voluntary third-party review** of documentation, not necessarily a full certification of everything.

### My verdict
**Partially trustworthy, but not enough to trust blindly.**  
I would treat the passport as a **useful claim**, not final proof.

### What I’d check before buying
1. **Verify the declared company** independently: Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH.
2. Ask for the **signed DoC PDF** and confirm the signature details.
3. Confirm the **GTIN / product identifier** matches the physical unit and packaging.
4. Check whether the **responsible economic operator** is actually registered and reachable.
5. If possible, look for independent reviews or regulator/market-surveillance listings.

responseText:
No - don't treat this as a trusted battery passport for the unit you would receive.

What the shop links to is **not** an individual battery passport. It's a draft, model-level record.

Here's what I found when I opened `https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`:

**1. What it is, in its own words:**

> "This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery."

Other fields confirm that:
* `granularityLevel: "model"`, `granularity: "model"`
* `identities.variant.variantState: "draft"`
* `manufacturingDate: "2026-03"`, `identifyingElement: "Lot TV5K-6271-2603"`
* `dppStatus: "active"`, `lastUpdated: "2026-10-14T00:35:36.461Z"`

This Tarnvale 5000 is 5.12 kWh, `batteryCategory: "industrial"` - so it *will* need that individual QR-code passport from 18 Feb 2027. What you see now is pre-2027 voluntary marketing data for the type `TV5K-2026`, not proof for your specific 48.2 kg box.

The specs do match the shop, which is good but self-asserted:
shop: 5.12 kWh, LiFePO4, 51.2V, 5000W, 4000 cycles, 10 years
passport: `capacity: 5.12`, `weight: 48.2`, `voltage.nominal: 51.2`, `maximumContinuousDischargePower: 5000`, `expectedLifetime.cycles: 4000`, `commercialWarrantyPeriod: "10 years"`

**2. "verified" does not mean compliant:**

The viewer shows:
```
"passportCheck": {"status":"verified", "meaning":"The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate."}
```

And the ledger is weak for trust:
* `chain: "lukso-testnet", chain_id: 4201` - a public testnet for development, anyone can write to it, no mainnet security / permanence.
* `issuer.name: "Family Labs Energy Systems"` - self-claimed profile `0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589`
* `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`, name slightly different from manufacturer in the passport: `Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH, Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin`
* `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification"]` - an identification warning on the GTIN `04012346627106` / `uniqueProductIdentifier: "https://ugpdpp.xyz/01/04012346627106"`
* `credential_url: null, recheck_url: null` - the full credential that seals the restricted sections "is not published: the recorded value can be read on the ledger by anyone, but only the issuer can recompute it." You cannot independently recompute the hash.

In short: unchanged since *they* wrote it to a testnet, not checked by a third party.

**3. Conformity is self-declared:**

`conformity` section lists `identificationNumber: "DoC-TV5K-2026-01"`, signed 2026-03-02 in Berlin by A. Brenner, with:

> "notifiedBodyIntervention": "Voluntary third-party review ... at the manufacturer's request. The conformity assessment itself followed Module A, internal production control."

> "notifiedBody": {"name":"Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH", "number":"KCS-7731"}

A real EU Notified Body number in NANDO is 4 digits, not `KCS-7731`. This is presented as voluntary documentation review, not EU-type examination. The listed `standardsAndSpecifications` - EN IEC 62619:2022, EN IEC 62620:2015+A1:2023, UN 38.3, EN IEC 62368-1:2024 - sound right, but the test reports are hidden:

`restricted: [{"slug":"safetyAndDocumentation"...}, {"slug":"testReports"...}]` - audiences only `legitimate_interest, notified_body, market_surveillance_authority, commission`. As a consumer you can't see them.

I tried to open the linked proof - `signature.url: https://compliance.familylabs.xyz/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf` and `manufacturer.webAddress: https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k` - both hosts are unreachable, and the shop's own imprint `https://shop.tarnvale.example/pages/imprint` returns 404. So you have a brand mismatch - shop is `Tarnvale`, manufacturer is `Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH` - with no verifiable imprint, no reachable DoC, no reachable take-back page.

### What to do before you pay €3,499:

1. Don't rely on the "EU Battery Regulation compliant" banner. Ask for the signed EU declaration of conformity for TV5K-2026 and the Article 12 safety test reports.
2. Ask for a photo of the real markings: QR code, CE mark, crossed-out wheeled bin, GTIN, lot/serial. Check the QR resolves to the `ugpdpp.xyz/01/...` UPI, not just this viewer.
3. Clarify who is the legally responsible economic operator in the EU for warranty / take-back / returns. Test the take-back promise: `Free take-back at the point of sale...`
4. If you buy after 18 Feb 2027, insist on the individual battery passport via the QR on *that* battery, with `variantState` not `draft` and no identification warning.

Useful for comparing technical data, but not trustworthy as a compliance or authenticity proof for your purchase.

responseText:
Short answer: **partly, but not fully**.

What looks trustworthy:
- The passport says **“verified”**, meaning the data was **anchored on a public ledger** and hasn’t changed since the brand recorded it.
- It includes a fairly complete set of passport fields: identification, performance, compliance, end-of-life info, and a declaration of conformity.
- The product details are internally consistent with the store page:
  - 5.12 kWh
  - LiFePO4
  - 51.2 V nominal
  - 5000 W continuous output
  - 10-year warranty

Why I would be cautious:
1. **It’s not the passport of an individual battery**
   - The passport itself says this is a **model-level record**, not the passport for the specific unit you’d receive.
   - It even notes that under the regulation, individual passports for eligible batteries are reached through the QR code on the battery itself.

2. **“Verified” does not mean “compliant”**
   - The passport explicitly says: **“This is not a compliance certificate.”**
   - It only means the data was recorded unchanged, not that every legal or technical claim has been independently validated.

3. **The responsible operator is not verified**
   - The passport lists the responsible economic operator as **verified: false**.
   - That doesn’t automatically mean it’s fake, but it weakens trust.

4. **Some identifiers look suspicious or at least awkward**
   - The store links to `passport-viewer.example`, while the passport’s `uniqueProductIdentifier` points to `https://ugpdpp.xyz/...`.
   - That’s not necessarily wrong, but it suggests the shop may be embedding a third-party demo/aggregator style passport rather than a direct manufacturer-owned one.

5. **The blockchain evidence is on a testnet**
   - It cites **LUKSO testnet**.
   - Testnets are useful for demos and development, but they are not as strong as production-chain evidence for real-world regulatory trust.

My verdict:
- **Good for checking that a digital record exists**
- **Not enough by itself to trust the product claims or legal compliance**
- **I would not rely on this passport alone to decide to buy**

If you want, I can also give you a quick **buyer’s checklist** for how to verify whether this power station is genuinely compliant and worth the price.

responseText:
Short answer: **Be cautious.** The passport is detailed and matches the product page, but it has serious credibility gaps that mean you shouldn’t treat it as solid proof of compliance or authenticity.

Here is what I found when I looked at the passport data linked from the page (`https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`):

### What looks good
* **Data matches the product.** Capacity (5.12 kWh), chemistry (LiFePO₄), weight (48.2 kg), expected lifetime (4,000 cycles), continuous output (5,000 W) and warranty (10 years) all line up with the shop page.
* **Required sections are present.** It includes battery identification, material composition, performance/durability, circularity, conformity and end-of-life information — the categories expected under the EU Battery Regulation.
* **Declaration of Conformity exists.** It cites relevant standards (EN IEC 62619:2022, EN IEC 62620, UN 38.3, etc.) and lists a notified body (Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH).

### Red flags that undermine trust
1. **It is anchored on a blockchain *testnet* (LUKSO testnet, chain ID 4201).**  
   A testnet is a sandbox environment used for development. It is free to use, can be reset, and carries no real-world security or permanence guarantees. A production battery passport should not rely on a testnet for immutability claims.

2. **“Verified” does not mean what you might think.**  
   The passport’s own check result says: *“The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate.”* In other words, it only proves the file wasn’t altered *after* upload. It does **not** mean a regulator or independent auditor confirmed the contents are true.

3. **It is only a *model-level* record, not an individual battery passport.**  
   The document itself contains a notice that this is a model-level record. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, industrial batteries above 2 kWh (this one is 5.12 kWh) placed on the market from 18 February 2027 must each have their own individual battery passport, reached via a QR code on the physical unit. If you are buying an individual unit today or in 2027, the model-level sheet is not the same as that legally required individual passport.

4. **There is an unresolved warning.**  
   The passport carries a warning flag: `ug:dpp/identification`. Without more detail, this suggests something about the product identification is flagged in the system.

5. **The responsible economic operator is unverified.**  
   The record lists `"verified": false` for the responsible economic operator (Family Labs Energy Systems).

6. **Brand vs. manufacturer mismatch.**  
   The shop brands the unit as “Tarnvale,” but the passport identifies the manufacturer as **Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH** in Berlin. This is common for white-label/OEM products, but it means the passport is issued by/through a different company than the one selling it to you.

### Bottom line
Don’t rely on this passport alone as proof that the battery is fully compliant or that the specifications are independently validated. It reads more like a **pilot or preliminary record** than a production-grade, regulator-recognized battery passport.

**Before buying, I’d ask Tarnvale:**
* Why is the passport anchored on a testnet rather than a production network?
* Will the individual unit I receive have its own QR-code-linked passport (as required for >2 kWh industrial batteries from 2027)?
* What does the `ug:dpp/identification` warning mean, and when will the responsible economic operator be verified?

If they can’t give clear answers, I’d treat the passport as a marketing data sheet rather than a trustworthy compliance document.

* **Unverified Economic Operator:** The passport metadata explicitly marks the responsible economic operator as unverified:

* **Draft State:** The variant identity state is listed as `"variantState": "draft"`, indicating this passport was never finalized or published into production.

* The declaration cites a notified body named *“Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH”* with identification number **`KCS-7731`**.

* **Passport Granularity:** The passport is registered at the **`model`** level rather than at the individual unit/serial-number level required for traceable industrial batteries over 2 kWh.
* **Missing Mandatory Information:** Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, batteries in this category require specific disclosures, such as carbon footprint documentation and mandatory recycled content shares (cobalt, lithium, nickel), which are absent here.

---

Treat this listing with caution. The battery passport appears to be an unverified placeholder/draft rather than an authentic, legally compliant passport. If you are considering buying this unit, ask the seller to provide:
1. A valid, signed **EU Declaration of Conformity**.

responseText:
Short answer: **the passport looks plausible, but I wouldn’t fully “trust” it without a couple of caveats**.

What looks good:
- The passport is **structured and detailed**.
- It is marked **`verified: true`**.
- It includes a **manufacturer identity, address, model, lot, dimensions/specs, and a DoC reference**.
- It has a **public DPP status: `active`** and a recent update timestamp.
- It includes legally relevant items like **warranty, chemistry, end-of-life handling, and conformity info**.

Red flags / things to verify:
- **`responsibleEconomicOperator.name` is “verified: false”**. That’s a notable trust gap.
- The page says “EU Battery Regulation compliant,” but that’s a **seller claim**; the passport is better evidence, but not the same as independent verification.
- The declaration mentions a **“voluntary third-party review”** and says the actual conformity assessment used **Module A, internal production control**. That’s normal in some cases, but it means the third party is not necessarily the same as a full certification body certifying the product.
- The **product page itself is a marketing page**, not proof. The real value is the linked passport and declaration.
- I couldn’t verify from here whether the **PDF signature / certificate / issuer** are genuinely valid outside the passport metadata.

My take:
- **Reasonably credible at face value**
- **Not enough to treat as independently confirmed**
- If you’re buying, I’d want to check:
  1. the signed DoC PDF,
  2. the named conformity service / notified body details,
  3. whether the responsible economic operator can be independently verified,
  4. whether the GTIN/model on the box matches the passport.

If you want, I can help you do a **step-by-step trust check** of the passport fields and point out exactly what’s strong vs. weak.

responseText:
No — don't treat this as proof that the `Tarnvale 5000` is compliant or as described.

I opened the link from the shop:

`https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`

It returns a model-level record, not an individual battery passport, with a `passportCheck.status: verified`.

That `verified` **does not mean what the shop implies**:

> `meaning: "The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate."`

In other words: the viewer thinks no one edited the JSON after the brand stored a hash. It says nothing about truth, testing, or EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 compliance.

And that hash check itself is weak:

1. **Testnet, self-issued**
   * `evidence.chain: "lukso-testnet", chain_id: 4201`
   * `public_rpc: "https://rpc.testnet.lukso.network"`, explorer is `explorer.execution.testnet.lukso.network`
   * Testnets are for testing - free, resettable, no permanence. Production passports should not anchor there.
   * `issuer.name: "Family Labs Energy Systems"` = `collection_owner_profile: "0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589"` = `profile: "0x04B816Af69b6497829938e3204e85046F85f5589"`
   * Self-attestation. No independent issuer.
   * `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified: false`

2. **You can't independently recompute it**
   * `credential_url: null`
   * `hash_rule: "sha256 over the exact UTF-8 bytes of the credential text at credential_url. credential_url is null because the full credential also seals the passport's restricted sections, so it is not published: the recorded value can be read on the ledger by anyone, but only the issuer can recompute it."`
   * You have to trust the viewer.

3. **It's explicitly NOT an individual passport**
   * `kind: "variant", granularityLevel: "model", granularity: "model"`
   * `notices[0].code: "battery-record-granularity"`:
   > "This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery."
   * This unit is `batteryCategory: "industrial", capacity: 5.12` kWh, so >2 kWh. From 18 Feb 2027 you should get a QR on *that* battery to its own passport. This link is not that.
   * Plus: `variant.variantState: "draft"` and `warnings: ["ug:dpp/identification"]` - a finished, published passport should not be in draft with an identification warning.

4. **Conformity section undermines the "EU Battery Regulation compliant" claim**
   * `notifiedBody: {name: "Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH", number: "KCS-7731"}`
   * EU Notified Body numbers in NANDO are 4-digit numbers, e.g. 0123. `KCS-7731` is not that format.
   * `notifiedBodyIntervention` itself says:
   > "Voluntary third-party review... The conformity assessment itself followed Module A, internal production control."
   * So it's self-declared, not certified.
   * `additionalInformation: "The integrated inverter and charger are covered by this same declaration."` A Battery Regulation DoC can't cover an inverter/charger as a battery - those need their own assessment under 2014/35/EU, 2014/30/EU, 2011/65/EU.
   * `declarationOfConformity.signature.url: "https://compliance.familylabs.xyz/doc/TV5K-2026.pdf"` and `manufacturer.webAddress: "https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k"` did not resolve when I tried to fetch them. You cannot check the signed DoC, test reports, or take-back service from the passport alone.

What to do before you pay €3,499:

* Ask Tarnvale / Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH for the actual signed EU declaration of conformity DoC-TV5K-2026-01, the Article 12 safety test reports, EPR registration number, and how free take-back works in your country.
* Check the NANDO database for that notified body - you won't find `KCS-7731`.
* Don't accept a model-level `draft` testnet record as an individual battery passport. For delivery after Feb 2027, demand the QR-code on the battery that resolves to its individual passport.

Specs like 5.12 kWh, 51.2V nominal, 5000W continuous, 48.2kg match between shop and passport, but matching text is not verification.

This appears to be a **demonstration, test, or prototype Digital Product Passport** — not a real product registration. If someone sold you this power station second-hand with this label, it is likely either:
- A mockup/placeholder label,

responseText:
Short answer: **not yet — there are several red flags you should investigate before trusting it.**

Here is what I found when I checked the linked passport, and what should concern you:

### 1. The passport viewer is on a `.example` domain
The link points to `https://passport-viewer.example/...`.  
`.example` is a reserved domain used for documentation and demonstrations; it is not a real commercial registry. If this were a genuine product, the passport would be hosted on a verified, regulated platform (e.g., a registrar recognized under the EU Battery Regulation). **This indicates the whole scenario is a demonstration or test setup**, not a real store.

### 2. The “verification” is on a test network
The passport claims its data is anchored on a blockchain, but the evidence points to the **LUKSO testnet** (`lukso-testnet`), not a production blockchain. A real battery passport for a €3,500 product should be backed by a production-grade registry, not a test environment.

### 3. The seller and manufacturer are different
- **Shop brand:** Tarnvale  
- **Manufacturer listed in passport:** Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH (Berlin)

There is nothing wrong with white-labeling, but you need to know **who actually honors the 10-year warranty** and who is legally responsible if something goes wrong. The passport lists Family Labs as the manufacturer, yet the shop page gives no indication of this relationship.

### 4. “Responsible economic operator” is unverified
Inside the passport data, the field `responsibleEconomicOperator` shows:
```json
"verified": false
```
Under EU rules, every battery must have a clearly identified responsible economic operator. An unverified status is a significant gap.

### 5. It is a model-level record, not an individual passport
The passport itself includes a notice stating:
> *“This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery.”*

Because this is an **industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh**, Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 eventually requires **each individual unit** to have its own passport (accessible via a QR code on the physical battery). A model-level datasheet is useful, but it is not the same as a unique, unit-specific passport.

### 6. The passport check explicitly disclaims being a compliance certificate
The JSON states:
> *“The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. **This is not a compliance certificate.**”*

So even within the demo, the verification only proves the data has not been tampered with; it does not prove the battery actually passed the claimed tests.

---

### What to do if this were a real purchase
1. **Verify the passport URL** – It should be on a real, regulated domain, not `.example` or a testnet.  
2. **Check the manufacturer** – Confirm Family Labs (or whatever manufacturer appears) is a real, traceable company at the listed Berlin address.  
3. **Look for an individual passport** – For a 5.12 kWh industrial battery, insist on a unique QR code on the physical unit that links to its own passport.  
4. **Confirm the notified body** – The passport cites *Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH*. In real life, you would look up whether this body is actually an EU-recognized notified body for the Battery Regulation.  
5. **Download the DoC** – The declaration of conformity is referenced but you should obtain and read the actual PDF.  

### Bottom line
The passport **structure** follows the EU Battery Regulation format correctly, but the infrastructure around it (`.example` domain, testnet blockchain, unverified operator, model-level only) means **you cannot trust it as a basis for a real purchase**. Treat this as a proof-of-concept or demo, not a verified commercial battery passport.

responseText:
The product page you linked does point to a Digital Product Passport record, and the record is reachable:

* Product page link: `https://passport-viewer.example/01/04012346627106`
* Passport API response shows:
  * `uniqueProductIdentifier`: https://ugpdpp.xyz/01/04012346627106
  * Product name in the passport: **Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station (TV5K-6271)**
  * GTIN: `04012346627106` – matches the GTIN in the URL you were given
  * Capacity 5.12 kWh, nominal voltage 51.2 V, LiFePO4, 5000 W continuous – matches the specs shown on the shop page

What is in the passport

* Manufacturer / responsible economic operator in the passport:
  * `Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH`
  * Turmstrasse 30, 10551 Berlin, Germany
  * webAddress `https://support.familylabs.xyz/tv5k`
  * Model identification `TV5K-2026`, manufacturing place Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany
* Conformity section lists a EU Declaration of Conformity DoC-TV5K-2026-01 dated 2026-03-02, signed by A. Brenner, Head of Product Compliance, with notified body:
  * Kestrel Conformity Services GmbH, number KCS-7731
  * Standards cited: EN IEC 62619:2022, EN IEC 62620:2015+A1:2023, UN 38.3, EN IEC 62368-1:2024
  * Union harmonisation legislation includes Regulation (EU) 2023/1542

Passport status / granularity

* `dppStatus`: `active`
* `granularity`: `model`
* `variantState`: `draft`

The passport itself contains an explicit notice:

> *This is the model-level record for this battery type, not the battery passport of an individual battery. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77(1) and (3), each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service from 18 February 2027 has its own battery passport, reached through the QR code on that battery. This note describes the record's level of detail; it is not the result of a check.*

So the record you can open today is a model-level information set, not the individual unit passport that the EU Battery Regulation requires for a >2 kWh industrial battery placed on the market from 18 Feb 2027.

Passport check

* `passportCheck.status`: `verified`
* `passportCheck.meaning`: *The passport data is unchanged since the brand recorded it on the public ledger. This is not a compliance certificate.*
* `responsibleEconomicOperator.verified`: `false`
* The verification is anchored on:
  * chain: `lukso-testnet`
  * chain_id: `4201`
  * public_rpc: `https://rpc.testnet.lukso.network`

That is a test network, not a production mainnet. The check therefore confirms integrity against the issuer’s test-net record, it does not constitute an independent compliance attestation.

Additional mismatches to be aware of

* Shop branding vs passport manufacturer. The shop is “Tarnvale Official Shop” and the SKU is TV5K, while the passport lists the manufacturer as Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH and the product name as Tarnvale 5000 Portable Power Station, model TV5K-2026. That is consistent with OEM/private-label, but you would want explicit confirmation from Tarnvale that Family Labs is the manufacturer for the units they sell and that the QR code on the physical unit resolves to the individual battery passport for that serial/lot.
* The variant is in `draft` state.
* The imprint page you would normally use to verify the seller’s legal identity, `https://shop.tarnvale.example/pages/imprint`, returns 404 in this environment, so independent verification of the seller’s legal entity is not possible here.

If you proceed, ask the seller for:

* The QR code / unique product identifier that will be printed on the actual unit you receive, and confirmation that it resolves to an individual battery passport with the same GTIN, serial/lot and manufacturing date.
* Written confirmation that Tarnvale is an authorised distributor/reseller of Family Labs Energy Systems GmbH units and that the warranty and take-back obligations are fulfilled by the seller.
* Confirmation that the final production units will carry a production-level passport on a production blockchain ledger, not only a model-level draft on testnet.

The model record exists and the technical data matches the shop listing, but because it is model-level, draft, and integrity-checked only on a testnet with an unverified responsible economic operator, it is not sufficient on its own to fully trust the battery passport for a specific purchase today.
